job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 Drafting Review: Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Vulnerabilities

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **§2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton cap applies "by a single vessel," so an operator could split production across several vessels, each staying under the limit, with no aggregation rule for common ownership or control.

2. **§2(1)(A), "metric tons" not specified as wet or dry.** Freshly recovered nodules hold substantial water, so wet versus dry weight could shift an operation across the threshold. The bill gives no measurement method or point of measurement (seabed, riser, or deck).

3. **§2(1)(A), "per year" undefined.** The bill doesn't say whether this means a calendar year, fiscal year, or rolling 12 months. That leaves room to time operations around period boundaries and makes the start of a violation hard to pin down.

4. **§2(1)(A), "recovery" undefined.** It is unclear whether recovery happens when nodules are collected on the seabed, lifted to the surface, or landed. An operator could argue that collector vehicles, riser systems, or transfer to a separate transport ship mean no single vessel "recovered" the material.

5. **§2(1)(A), "vessel" and "mineral resources" undefined.** Operations from fixed platforms or other non-vessel structures may fall outside the definition. "Other mineral resources" is broad enough to arguably cover sand, gravel, or hydrocarbons, which invites overbreadth objections and narrowing constructions.

6. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary" never defined.** No section identifies which Secretary (Commerce, Interior, or another), so the provision's main discretionary authority has no clear holder.

7. **§2(1)(B), open-ended "comparable risks" standard.** Letting an official expand the scope of a crime by determination, with no criteria, procedure, or rulemaking requirement, invites void-for-vagueness challenges (given the 10-year criminal penalty) and nondelegation challenges.

8. **§2(2), narrow "U.S. person" definition.** The definition covers only citizens and corporations organized under State law. It omits lawful permanent residents, LLCs and partnerships (arguably), foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies, and possibly D.C. or territorial entities, since "State" is undefined. A U.S. parent could operate abroad through a foreign subsidiary.

9. **§2(3), "covered vessel" thresholds.** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less escape registration. A vessel that removes or swaps out recovery equipment between voyages could argue it is not "equipped for" recovery when the requirement applies.

10. **§2(3) vs. §2(1)(A), mismatched vessel concepts.** The prohibition uses "vessel" while the registry uses "covered vessel," so a vessel subject to the mining ban may never be registered or monitored.

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

11. **§3(a), "in the United States" undefined geographically.** The bill doesn't say whether this includes the territorial sea, EEZ, or continental shelf. Foreign companies on foreign-flagged vessels in the U.S. EEZ may fall outside the prohibition.

12. **§3(a), no ban on financing, sponsoring, purchasing, importing, or processing.** U.S. companies could fund, contract for, buy, or process nodules mined by foreign entities, and there is no import prohibition.

13. **§3(a), "person" undefined.** The bill doesn't say whether "person" includes government entities, foreign governments, or state-owned enterprises.

14. **§3(b), exploration-license exemption is ambiguous and open-ended.** It exempts "mining conducted under an exploration license," which could be read to grandfather full commercial recovery by any existing license holder. It doesn't say who must have issued the license (NOAA under DSHMRA, the ISA, or a foreign sponsoring state), and it doesn't address expiration, renewal, extension, transfer, or expansion of licensed areas.

15. **§3(b), no treatment of existing commercial recovery permits or pending applications.** The bill doesn't say whether NOAA must stop processing DSHMRA permits or how the bill interacts with DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.). That leaves implied-repeal questions open, and affected parties could raise takings arguments.

16. **§3(c), environmental-assessment exemption has no limits.** The term is undefined and has no tonnage cap, permit requirement, oversight, or limit on selling recovered material. Any operation could claim a dual "assessment" purpose, including large pilot mining tests.

## Sec. 4: Registry

17. **§4, no penalty for noncompliance.** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register or report, or filing a false report, carries no penalty under the Act. 18 U.S.C. 1001 might reach false statements, but that is untested here.

18. **§4(a)–(b), no deadlines, required content, or verification.** The bill sets no registration deadline. Reports need only "describe" activities, with no required data on tonnage, location, depth, or buyers. Certification is self-certification, with no observers, vessel monitoring, or audits.

19. **§4, applies to all covered vessels worldwide.** It has no U.S. nexus requirement such as flag, port, or operator nationality, which invites extraterritoriality and international-law objections and is practically unenforceable against foreign operators.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

20. **§5(a), conflicts with §8 effective date.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. This creates confusion about liability during the gap and possible retroactivity objections.

21. **§5(a), daily penalty vs. annual threshold.** A violation exists only once a vessel exceeds 10,000 tons in a year. It is unclear which "day" the violation occurs on, and whether earlier days in the year count.

22. **§5, no enforcement machinery.** No agency is given authority to assess penalties, inspect, board, subpoena, or seize. There are no notice-and-hearing procedures, no judicial review provision, no forfeiture of vessels or minerals, and no Coast Guard role.

23. **§5(a), Seventh Amendment exposure.** If an agency assesses these large civil penalties administratively, *SEC v. Jarkesy* (2024) supports a jury-trial challenge. The bill doesn't specify a judicial forum.

24. **§5(b), "willfully" standard.** This requires proof that the defendant knew the conduct was unlawful, which is hard to establish given the bill's undefined terms.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

25. **§6, unclear and unenforceable mandate.** It is unclear whether the 18-month deadline applies to beginning negotiations or concluding an agreement. The section has no reporting requirement or consequence, and it doesn't address the complication that the U.S. is not a party to UNCLOS.

## Sec. 7: Duration

26. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), conflicting termination provisions.** Subsection (a) continues the prohibition until a joint resolution is passed, while (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years. Which controls is unclear.

27. **§7(a), mechanism is hollow.** No provision directs anyone to commission the National Academies report, "serious harm" is undefined, and a joint resolution is ordinary legislation that Congress could pass anyway. The clause does no independent legal work.

28. **§7(b), sunset runs from enactment, not effective date.** Combined with §8, the prohibition actually lasts only about 9.5 years. The bill also doesn't say whether pending enforcement actions survive the sunset (1 U.S.C. 109 likely preserves accrued penalties, but the bill is silent).

## Sec. 8 and Structural Issues

29. **§8, 180-day delay.** The delay opens a window to accelerate recovery. Read with §3(b), it also creates an incentive to obtain licenses before enactment.

30. **No severability clause.** Given the vulnerability of §2(1)(B), the extraterritorial provisions, and the penalty structure, a successful challenge to one provision could put the whole Act at risk.

31. **No rulemaking authority.** No agency is authorized to issue implementing regulations to define terms, set measurement methods, or run the registry. Courts would have to resolve these ambiguities case by case.

**Most consequential items:** #1, #14, #16, #17, #6/#7, #11–12, and #26. These are where the bill's core coverage or enforceability is weakest.
